name: Unit Roster
description:
Who is on the board, which side they are on, which tile they stand on, and how much of them is left. Every tactics component asks one of those three questions and none of them owned the answer: the turn queue rolls initiative per combatant, the movement range floods out from a unit's tile, and cover is priced between an attacker and a defender. Each was written as though somebody else held the roster, and nobody did.

A unit is an identity with a position, not a position with a name. That is why moving is an event this component hears rather than a field a caller writes: movement.grid_movement_range decides which tiles are legal and announces the move, this records where the unit now is, and the two cannot disagree because only one of them is allowed to answer. The same rule ends a unit -- combat.damage_resolver announces the defeat, and removal is this component reacting to it rather than the resolver reaching across.

Stats live here because they are per unit and consulted by everyone: the queue wants a dexterity to break ties, the range wants a movement allowance, the resolver wants hit points. It is deliberately not a character sheet -- progression.attribute_sheet owns the RPG one -- and deliberately not a party: social.party_formation is about who you bring, this is about who is standing here now. A run that crosses between regions tears the whole build down and rebuilds it, so anything a player earned has to be handed to the next build through a DECLARED input or it is silently lost — which is how an RPG hands back a fresh character every time you walk off the edge of the map. That is what the initial-state input below is for: it is the same rule economy.currency's startingBalance follows, and it is a request's business to supply, never this component's to remember. A unit ARRIVING follows the same rule as a unit moving and a unit dying: it is an event this component hears, not a write somebody else performs. combat.spawn_director decides that a region needs another hostile and announces it; this is what admits it to the board. Any other arrangement gives the board two authors, and two authors is how a spawner and a roster end up disagreeing about how many things are in the room.

implementations.note: Implemented in the consuming application; not verifiable from this repository.

inputs.name: units
inputs.description: The starting board: id, team, tile x and y, and stats. Required, because a roster with a default is somebody else's battle.

inputs.name: teams
inputs.description: Sides, in the order they are offered a turn when initiative ties all the way down. Two is the genre default; three is a free-for-all.

inputs.name: removeOnDefeat
inputs.description: Whether a defeated unit leaves the board. False keeps the body as an obstacle, which some games use as cover and most do not want.

inputs.name: blockOccupiedTiles
inputs.description: Whether a unit's tile is impassable to others. Off for games where units stack or pass through allies -- but the frontline stops meaning anything.

inputs.name: defaultHealth
inputs.description: Health for a unit whose own record does not state one. A roster already owns whether a unit is standing; health is that same fact at more resolution, and keeping the two together is what stops a second component deciding a unit is dead while this one still lists it. A unit record may override it per unit — a boar is not a wolf.

inputs.name: initialHealth
inputs.description: Remaining health per unit id, applied over whatever the `units` list says. It exists because health and POSITION have opposite lifetimes across a region crossing: the level decides where everyone stands in the new region, and the player's remaining health is the one thing that must survive from the old one. Carrying the whole units array instead would drag the previous region's enemies along with it.

outputs.name: units
outputs.description: Live roster: id, team, x, y, and stats.

outputs.name: teams
outputs.description: The sides, in the order they were declared. First is the one a player is expected to be holding, which is the convention everything that has to tell the two apart already needs: a fog of war reveals around one side's units, and an AI takes turns for the others. Publishing it means both read the same answer instead of each picking a rule.

outputs.name: unitAt
outputs.description: The unit standing on a tile, or null.

outputs.name: positionOf
outputs.description: The tile a unit id stands on, or null once it is gone.

outputs.name: aliveByTeam
outputs.description: Survivors per team, which is what a victory condition counts.

outputs.name: healthOf
outputs.description: Remaining and maximum health per living unit id. Published because a damage resolver has to know what it is chipping at, and the alternative — every attacker carrying the defender’s health in its payload — asks the attacker to know something only the board knows.

outputs.name: damage
outputs.description: Apply damage to a unit id and report what happened: remaining health, and whether that killed it. The caller owns the NUMBER (combat.damage_resolver computes mitigation, crit and variance); this owns the consequence.
